title: Doing well? — asking and saying no
goal: Make yes-or-no questions with the *có … không?* frame, negate with *không* and *không phải*, and answer questions in a language that has no word for "yes".
bekal: build yes-or-no questions with *có … không?* and *… phải không?*
negate verbs with *không* and nouns with *không phải*

notes: **Có … không? is the most important question frame in all of Vietnamese.** What you're asking about is sandwiched between *có* and *không*: *Chị **có** rảnh **không**?* Literally "you **have** free **not**?" — a bit like "free or not?". In casual speech *có* is often dropped: *Chị rảnh không?*

**Vietnamese has no word for "yes".** *Vâng* and *dạ* don't mean "yes" but "right, as you say" — they agree with **the way the question was put**, not with the facts. The most natural way to answer is to **repeat the verb**: *Chị có rảnh không?* is answered *Rảnh.* (free) or *Không rảnh.* (not free).

**Không has two jobs to keep apart.** **Before a verb or adjective** it means "not": *tôi không rảnh*. At **the end of a sentence** it's part of the question frame. And to negate **a noun** it isn't enough on its own — you use *không phải*: *Không phải.* = "No, it isn't."

**Phải không? at the end of a sentence = "right?"** Literally "right or not?", and it does exactly the job of English tag questions ("…, isn't it?", "…, right?"): it offers a guess and asks for confirmation. Its cousins are *à?* and *hả?* — *à* is soft, because the speaker has just realized something; *hả* is blunter and a little surprised.

**Chưa means "not yet", and it's a complete answer.** *Dạ chưa.* is a full sentence. Note that *chưa* isn't an ordinary negation: it leaves the door open, like "not yet" — and answering "married?" with "not yet" sounds far more polite in Vietnamese than answering "no".

**Mà at the end of a sentence = "…, you know!" or "after all".** It gently objects, reminding the listener of something they should already know: *Tôi còn đi học mà!* = "I'm still a student, you know!" Little words like this turn your Vietnamese from correct into alive; the full set is in Unit 17.

grammars.title: Four yes-or-no question frames
body: All of them are made by **adding words**; none by changing the word order. A statement and a question have exactly the same order — unlike English, which flips the sentence ("you are" → "are you?").
after: ⚠️ **Don't mix *có … không?* with question words.** If the sentence already has *gì*, *đâu*, *ai* or *nào*, the *có … không?* frame is **not used**: *Chị làm việc ở đâu?* — not *Chị có làm việc ở đâu không?*. Just as in English you don't say "do you work where or not?".

*Có* on its own also means "there is" and "to have" — *tôi có hai con* = "I have two children". So when you see *có* mid-sentence without *không* at the end, it's working as an ordinary verb, not as a question marker.

grammars.title: Answering without "yes"
body: Since there's no word for "yes", answers are built from **the question's own verb**. It feels odd for two days, then far more sensible than "yes".
after: ⚠️ **Vâng agrees with how the question was put, not with the facts**, and that's a hidden trap with negative questions. *Anh không đi à?* ("You're not coming?") answered with *Vâng* means "right, I'm not coming" — not "yes, I'm coming". If you are coming, answer *Có, tôi đi.*
Answering by repeating the verb is always safe and always clear. If you can't decide between *vâng* and *không*, just repeat the verb — that's what native speakers do most of the time.

What it negates
Example
rows: *Tôi **không phải là** bác sĩ.* — I'm not a doctor.
*Không xa **đâu**!* — It's not far at all!

blocks.text: Each of these matches an English idea one to one: *không* = not, *không phải* = isn't (a…), *chưa* = not yet, *đừng* = don't!, *chẳng* = no way / not at all, *không … đâu* = not … at all. None is a new concept — all you need to learn is how they sound.

blocks.title: One question you'll hear every day
items: *Ăn cơm chưa?* — literally "eaten rice yet?". It's a greeting, not a real question, much like "How's it going?" — nobody is offering you lunch. Answer *Rồi, cảm ơn.* or *Chưa*, whichever is true.
Its cousin: *Đi đâu đấy?* — "where are you off to?" — also just a greeting. An answer like *Đi chơi thôi.* ("just going out") is enough and isn't considered evasive.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Được không?* is one of the most useful sentences in all of Vietnamese: two words, meaning "may I?", "can you?" and "OK?" all at once. You can tack it onto almost anything — point at the item, say the number, then *được không?* The word *được* has its own unit, Unit 12.
